subject: How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?

messages.author: 2330bbb33122f310
messages.subject: How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
parts:
Dear all

I have a question om modeling strategy:

My data are basically areas of located farms. That is for each observed location I know the magnitude of an area around it, but not the shape. Actually, the observed areas are not exactly what I want. Rather I should have the fraction of farm area relative to all area. The problem is how to extract this information.

A first idea is to take a square of area A around each observation point, and take the sum of observed areas within the square relative to A as an approximate fraction. In turn the fraction or its log can be used as observation. Another approach could be to translate to binomial data and let 1-s weighted with farm area fraction and 0-s weighted with 1-fraction be the INLA-observations. The appropriate size of A need to be guessed for suitable smoothing.

Another idea is to utilize the mesh. Each node of the inner part of the mesh can be taken as observation nodes where the non-farm area of the surrounding triangles are located. The data should then be considered binomial as above. I see that the calculation of the non-farm area for each node is somewhat technical, but more precise locations of the non-farm area can posssibly be obtained in this way. The range parameter of the SPDE need to be guessed for suitable smoothing. I do not necessarily need precise information in areas with no farmland, but in these cases I might just as well impute NAs.

What do you think? Are there other altternatives?

best
Øyvind

parts:
Hi,

Can you clarify what you’re observing, as I get the impression that it’s not the farm sizes that you’re modelling, but rather that the farm sizes are relevant to what you’re observing (e.g. if the observations are something like “number of trees”). How the farm sizes would be used depends entirely on why they are relevant!

Finn

messages.author: 2330bbb33122f310
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
parts:
You are right, Finn. I am not modelling the farm sizes.

The object of the analysis is the grain crop yield per ha and the impact of distances to centers. I observe areas of crop land, areas with grain crop, and total grain yield for specific farm locations. I also observe center location for calculation of straight distance to nearest center. The hypotheses from economics is that longer distance means lower profit per ha, lower input intensity and lower yields. The problem from causal analysis is that low fractions of crop land in general and crop land used for grain in particular (relative to all land) are possible confounders for both distance to center and yield per ha. One should at least try to correct for this in order to find the causal effect of distance.

I guess there might be similar cases in disease mapping when the concentration of people affects the infection rates? One would then need not only observation of infections but also non-infections?

Øyvind

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
parts:
I see. Rereading the original message with this in mind, it seems to em you have a very tricky problem, in that you need information about area fractions at locations where it wasn’t measures, and the locations where you do have measurements might themselves be confounded with those fractions (depending on how the spatial observation design was made). The idea of modelling the fraction (which might be less confounded than the absolute areas) as a spatial field seems like a reasonable compromise to me. However, I wasn’t able to follow the details of what your idea for how to do that; perhaps that’s because the area measurements lack information about the locations where you don’t have measurements?

Finn

messages.author: 2330bbb33122f310
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
parts:
Thanks, Finn.

As presumed, I am slightly off the broad track of INLA-SPDE modelling. Anyway, I guess nothing but INLA-SPDE will carrry me through. 

Some more explicit reasoning: Assume some resource is uniformly spread in space, and that centers are formed to gather a certain amount of that resource with a minimum of transportation costs. Centers will then arise in a triangular grid. Distance between centers --- and average distance to center alike --- will then depend on the concentration of the resource. If the study variable possibly depends both on the concentration and the distance to center, a measure of concentration is required in the causal regression model. In some way it can be deduced from the observations of the resource. The question is how. A first point to note: I have no interest in low-range SPDE fields of concentration. These will not affect center locations to large extent. It is the long-range fields that will. Moreover the relevant range should be sufficiently large to cover 3-4 centers on average. Else the correlation between concentration and distance will be weak.

This analysis has implications for the modelling. Either I could calculate concentration within squares covering the neighborhoods of approximately 4 centers for each observation, and take these as covariates, or I could measure concentration  in some more detail and extract the relevant information with a sufficiently long-range SPDE-field.The covariate approach makes the model smaller. I would in any case need an SPDE-field for the residuals of the regression. 2-3 additional fields for the regressors plus stocastic regression parameters lead to a pretty large model.

Preliminary conclusion is that my first proposal is simplest and preferrable.

best
Øyvind
